title: The three pages that broke knowledge
teaches: Justified true belief and Gettier's 1963 counterexamples

blocks.text: In 1963 Edmund Gettier was a young philosopher at Wayne State University in Detroit. His colleagues told him he needed to publish something if he wanted to keep his job. He had an idea he had been discussing with them, and wrote it up in a paper less than three pages long, "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?", in the journal *Analysis*. It is one of the most discussed papers in 20th-century philosophy. Gettier hardly published anything else in the rest of his long career; he is said to have explained that he had nothing more to say.[^gettier]

The paper attacked a definition of knowledge that goes back, in a form, to Plato. In the *Theaetetus*, a dialogue by Plato, Socrates and a young mathematician try out the idea that knowledge is true belief with an account, a reason that backs it up. Later philosophers called this condition **justification**. The idea became standard. To know something, you must believe it; it must be true; and you must be justified in believing it, have good reason for it. Knowledge is **justified true belief**.

blocks.caption: The traditional analysis of knowledge. Each condition seems necessary; the question is whether together they are enough.

steps.text: You believe it. (You cannot know what you do not believe.)
It is true. (You cannot know what is false.)
You are justified in believing it. (A lucky guess is not knowledge.)
A belief can meet all three conditions and still be true only by luck.

blocks.text: Gettier's first case is about a job. Smith and Jones have both applied. Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get it: the company president told him so. He has also counted the coins in Jones's pocket: ten. So Smith believes that Jones will get the job and Jones has ten coins in his pocket, and from that he infers: "The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket." That belief is justified, since he inferred it correctly from good evidence.

In fact, Smith gets the job, not Jones. And, without knowing it, Smith also has ten coins in his own pocket. So the man who gets the job, Smith himself, does have ten coins, and Smith's belief that the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket is true, and justified. But it is true by luck, not because of his evidence, which was all about Jones. Almost everyone agrees that Smith did not know it. So justified true belief is not enough for knowledge.

Simpler cases make the same point. Bertrand Russell had described one in 1948: someone looks at a clock that says three o'clock, and believes it is three. The clock has stopped, but by chance it stopped exactly twelve hours ago, so his belief is true, and it is justified, since the clock has always been reliable.

blocks.caption: Russell's stopped clock. Your answer is saved on the Verdicts page.

options.ask: A woman glances at a clock she has always relied on and believes it is three o'clock. It is three o'clock, but the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago. Does she know it is three?
choices: No: she is right only by luck
Yes: she has a justified true belief
who: You chose the answer almost everyone gives, which is Gettier's point.
You chose the traditional analysis. On that view she knows, though her evidence had nothing to do with why she is right.
Some philosophers think the intuition is weaker than it looks.

blocks.text: Once people saw the pattern, cases were easy to make. The recipe is to take a justified belief that would normally be false, then add a stroke of luck that makes it true anyway. The oldest known example comes from India. Around 770 AD the Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara[^dharmottara] described a traveller in the desert who sees a shimmer of water ahead. It is a mirage, but when he reaches the spot there is water there, under a rock.

blocks.caption: Six beliefs. Sort each by whether it is knowledge, a true belief that is right by luck, or simply false.

items.name: You check a working clock and believe it is noon. It is noon.
items.why: Justified, true, and true because of your evidence.

items.name: You read in a reliable newspaper that the match was won 2 to 1, and it was.
items.why: Good testimony that tracks the truth.

items.name: You see what looks like a sheep in a field; it is a dog in a fleece, but a real sheep is hidden behind a wall.
items.why: Roderick Chisholm's case: there is a sheep in the field, but not the one you saw.

items.name: Driving through a county full of fake barn fronts, you see the one real barn and believe it is a barn.
items.why: The fake barns case: in that county you could easily have been fooled.

items.name: A traveller sees a mirage of water, and finds real water under a rock at the spot.
items.why: Dharmottara's case, about 1,200 years before Gettier.

items.name: You see a clock that runs an hour slow and believe it is noon. It is one o'clock.
items.why: Justified, but not true, so not knowledge on any view.

blocks.text: Philosophers spent decades trying to add a fourth condition. One proposal was that the belief must not be inferred from anything false. That rules out Smith, whose belief was inferred from a false one, but not the fake barns case, where nothing false is believed at all. Another was that the fact must cause the belief in the right way, but the one real barn does cause your belief. Alvin Goldman's **reliabilism** said a belief is knowledge if it was produced by a process that reliably produces true beliefs, which handles the barns, since your eyes are not reliable among fakes, but met counterexamples of its own. Later views say a known belief must be **safe**: it could not easily have been false.

Every proposal met new counterexamples. In 1994 Linda Zagzebski argued that this will always happen as long as the justification condition allows any chance of error, since luck can always fill the gap between good reasons and truth. Timothy Williamson, the epistemicist of branch lesson K3, proposed in 2000 that the project was the wrong way round: knowledge is basic and cannot be defined in simpler terms, and belief and justification should be explained by it, not the reverse.

Experimental philosophers, who test philosophers' intuitions with surveys of ordinary people, have asked whether ordinary people share the intuition. A small study in 2001 suggested that people from East Asian and South Asian backgrounds were more likely than Westerners to say Gettier's characters knew. A larger study in 2017, with people in Brazil, India, Japan and the United States, found no such difference: in every group tested, most people judged that the lucky believer did not know.

Gettier's point is accepted almost everywhere: justified true belief is not sufficient for knowledge. What knowledge is instead is still argued over, and the main contenders are versions of reliabilism, safety, virtue theories, on which knowledge is true belief that comes from the believer's skill and not luck, and Williamson's knowledge-first view. The traditional analysis is respected history. The paper itself is a model for philosophers of how much one clear counterexample can do.

blocks.caption: Four questions on Gettier
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What was the traditional definition Gettier attacked?
choices: Knowledge is true belief that no one could doubt
Knowledge is belief produced by a reliable process
Knowledge is true belief that experts would endorse
items.why: Its roots go back to Plato's Theaetetus.

items.ask: What is the point of Gettier's ten coins case?
choices: Smith's belief is justified and true, but true by luck, so it is not knowledge
Smith's belief is justified but false, so it is not knowledge
Smith's belief is true, but he had no good evidence for it
Smith's belief is knowledge, which shows the traditional view is right
items.why: His evidence was all about Jones, but the belief was made true by facts about Smith.

items.ask: Which of these is a Gettier case?
choices: Seeing a dog in a fleece and believing there is a sheep in the field, when a real sheep is hidden from view
Checking a working clock and believing correctly that it is noon
Believing it is noon from a clock that is an hour slow
Believing a reliable newspaper's correct match report
items.why: Chisholm's case: the belief is true, but not because of what you saw.

items.ask: What did Williamson propose in response to Gettier?
choices: Knowledge is basic and cannot be defined in simpler terms
Knowledge is justified true belief with no false steps
Knowledge is true belief produced by a reliable process
Knowledge is true belief that could not easily have been false
items.why: His knowledge-first view reverses the order of explanation.

summary: **Gettier's 1963 paper was less than three pages long.** It is among the most discussed in modern philosophy.
**The traditional view: knowledge is justified true belief.** Its roots are in Plato's Theaetetus.
**A belief can be justified and true by luck.** Smith and the ten coins; the stopped clock.
**Dharmottara described such a case around 770 AD.** A mirage, with real water under a rock.
**Every fourth condition proposed met new counterexamples.** Causal theories, reliabilism and safety.
**Williamson: knowledge cannot be defined in simpler terms.** Knowledge comes first.
**The intuition seems to be shared across cultures.** An early study suggested otherwise; a larger one in 2017 found it in four countries.

gettier.title: The man of one paper
gettier.text: Gettier taught for decades at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and died in 2021. He worked on logic and other questions, but rarely published, and seemed content to be known for three pages.

dharmottara.title: Gettier cases before Gettier
dharmottara.text: Dharmottara's examples were brought to wide attention by historians of Indian philosophy, among them Bimal Krishna Matilal. Similar cases have been found in the 14th-century Italian writer Peter of Mantua. None of them led to a debate like the one Gettier started.
